MARKET.head: Bordeaux leads trade as Lynch-Bages 2005 becomes top-traded wine
MARKET.summ: US and UK buyers both upped their purchasing, the former segment reclaiming their share of purchasing
takeaways: Bordeaux held the lead with a 37.4% share of purchases, and Lynch-Bages was the region's top-traded wine.
Burgundy's share fell to 15.4% from 18.4% the prior week, below a September average of 24.6%.
US buyers drove purchasing, with their share of trade rising from 7.0% to 9.6% week on week.

MARKET.head: Surrey backs 17 rural innovation projects with £500,000 in grants
MARKET.summ: A wine producer using bird-repelling lasers and cattle farmer using GPS collars to track livestock are among 17 innovative projects funded from a £500,000 pot to boost Surrey’s rural economy. Surrey County Council’s Farming Innovation Accelerator supports farmers and growers with funding for projects to modernise operations,...
takeaways: Surrey County Council's Farming Innovation Accelerator funded 17 projects from a £500,000 pot of UK Shared Prosperity Funding.
Over 50 organisations applied, and each of the 17 chosen recipients receives a grant of up to £35,000 plus expert support.
Albury Vineyard will install an automated bird-repellent laser to protect 18 acres of grapevines, adding over 1,700 bottles a year.

MARKET.head: VinePair weekly roundup spans Supreme Court case, Uncle Nearest sale, and new releases
MARKET.summ: This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Diageo’s toxic chemical spill, SCOTUS to review a home distilling case, the latest product releases, and more.
takeaways: The US Supreme Court agreed to review a home distilling case, according to VinePair's weekly roundup of beverage alcohol news.
The roundup also covers potential buyers for Uncle Nearest, the whiskey brand led by founder Fawn Weaver.
Diageo's toxic chemical spill and Southern Glazer's bribery case were among the week's other industry headlines.

CULTURE.head: Volcanic soils give wines a distinctive tension, importers and writers say
CULTURE.summ:
Vines on volcanic soil are hard to grow and their grapes are hard-won, but it all combines to produce wines with a very particular sense of place

Good stories need jeopardy. Take The Princess Bride, one of my favourite films, which I recently introduced...
takeaways: Volcanic wines come from soils such as ash, basalt, obsidian, pumice and tuff, which vary widely in character.
Importer Nic Rizzi of Modal Wines says volcanic wines carry an extra tension that is hard to describe.
Victoria Torres Pecis farms La Palma in the Canaries, where black ash soils, high vineyards and low-trained vines are used.

CULTURE.head: Germany's Chardonnays gain recognition as warming climate ripens the grape
CULTURE.summ: Riesling is all but synonymous with German wine. It’s the most planted grape in Germany, accounting for almost a quarter of the country’s vineyard area. And while Riesling’s dominance is not about to change anytime soon, another white variety is becoming recognized for its quality and potential in Germany.
takeaways: Germany's Chardonnay covers about 3 percent of its vineyards, around 7,000 acres in 2023, and is growing.
Importer Collin Wagner says Chardonnay is easier for drinkers to understand than Riesling, which carries more baggage.
Warmer southwest regions Rheinhessen, Pfalz and Baden now ripen the grape in most years, with bottles priced around $40 to $60.

CULTURE.head: Ohio buyer finds 400 pre-1940 bottles in 1939-sealed mansion cellar
CULTURE.summ: John Smith had to actually buy the 10,600-square-foot stucco Tudor mansion before he would be able to open the wine cellar and find out what bottles had been left down there some 86 years earlier. Hidden off the main road at the end of a circular driveway, The Sherman Estates was built on fifteen acres of land in northwest...
takeaways: John Smith bought Dayton's 1925 Sherman Estates mansion and opened its cellar, sealed since John Q. Sherman died in 1939.
He found about 400 bottles, all from the 1930s or earlier, including Niersteiner Rhine wine from 1895 and Cuban rum from around 1919.
Smith sold one opened, half-full Bacardi bottle to the company for $1,000; its heritage curator said the find was like Christmas.

CULTURE.head: Plumpton College recruits Level 3 viticulture apprentices for November 9 intake
CULTURE.summ: Develop the skills your business needs, invest in emerging talent and help shape the future of the UK wine industry with a Viticulture Apprenticeship at Plumpton College. As the UK wine industry continues to grow, developing a skilled workforce is essential to its long-term success. Plumpton College’s Level 3 Viticulture...
takeaways: Plumpton College is recruiting its next Level 3 Viticulture Apprenticeship cohort, starting 9 November, with late joiners possibly accepted in January.
For eligible non-levy-paying SMEs, 100% of training costs are government-funded for apprentices aged 16 to 24, subject to funding rules.
The apprenticeship combines workplace experience with block weeks of college learning, and qualifications are endorsed by WineGB.

CULTURE.head: Navarra turns costly rosé methods into a premium identity; English wine could follow
CULTURE.summ: How Navarra Rosado turned production challenges into premium positioning and a compelling marketing story. Andrea Ontiveros Flores, a sommelier and marketing & communications specialist from Alicante, Spain asks if English wine could do the same? Consumers rarely pay more simply because winemaking is difficult.
takeaways: Navarra rosado's premium standing rests on the Saignée method, which needs up to three times more grapes than standard red production.
Navarra introduced the Rosado Tradition designation, requiring Saignée and exclusive Garnacha, to protect that identity.

SCIENCE.head: Oak alternatives' timing and goals shape colour stability and aroma in winemaking
SCIENCE.summ: Oak remains one of the most powerful tools available to winemakers for shaping wine style, structure, and complexity. While traditional barrel ageing continues to play an important role, modern oak alternatives offer greater flexibility, lower cost, and increased precision when used with a clearly defined objective.
takeaways: Oak chips added during active fermentation barely improve colour stability because oxygen availability is very low.
Colour benefits peak during maturation when oak is combined with controlled oxygen exposure such as micro-oxygenation.
Greater oak surface area releases aroma faster, and lightly, medium or heavily toasted oak yields distinct aroma profiles.

SCIENCE.head: English vineyards hit by 2026 frosts, then record heat and drought
SCIENCE.summ: With harvest complete, or nearing completion on many vineyards, Hutchinsons agronomists Rob Saunders and Will Robinson look at the impact of the record-breaking summer and what we can learn for future seasons. While 2026 could be remembered as a vintage season for some growers, others will look back less fondly, having first...
takeaways: Fifty-four UK Met Office stations broke their all-time daily maximum temperature records during summer 2026, with 38.2°C recorded in Gloucestershire in August.
Heat effects on vines varied by age, rainfall and variety, with older vines more resilient and Bacchus struggling most with intense heat and UV.
Harvest came 10-14 days early on average, but sugar development stalled while acidity kept falling on many sites.

SCIENCE.head: UK vineyards face early, warm, dry 2026 harvest after frost-hit start
SCIENCE.summ: After a run of dramatically different vintages, 2026 has given UK viticulture another season that challenged assumptions, but also demonstrated just how much English and Welsh vineyards can achieve. The 2026 growing season began with a series of extraordinary frost events, creating a challenging start before developing into a...
takeaways: The 2026 English and Welsh growing season began with severe frost, then turned warm, dry and fast-ripening.
Harvest arrived several weeks early at some vineyards, and dry weather kept disease pressure low.
Growers say no typical season can be planned for now, so soil health, water management and monitoring matter more.

SCIENCE.head: Domaine Bousquet details its organic and water-saving practices in Mendoza
SCIENCE.summ: Domaine Bousquet continues to elevate Argentine wine through generations of dedication and innovation in organic wine practices. Earlier this year, Irma Remigio and her team warmly welcomed SWR’s Membership Manager, Ilva Fridenberga, to their winery. The winery, located at the foot of the Andes Mountains, is globally recognized...
takeaways: SWR Membership Manager Ilva Fridenberga visited Domaine Bousquet's winery at the foot of the Andes in February.
The winery is trialing biodiversity corridors, closed to disturb vegetation, and garden corridors growing vegetables between vine rows.
It switched to high-pressure hoses to cut water use and upgraded tanks, cooling and sorting machinery to save energy.

SCIENCE.head: Portuguese trial cuts vine yields with ethephon and manual thinning in Loureiro and Borraçal
SCIENCE.summ: Some years, climate conditions and biological events increment the fertility of vines, which can lead to over cropping and a decrease of wine quality
takeaways: A 2007 experiment in two Vinhos Verdes vineyards tested yield control on Loureiro and Borraçal grape varieties.
Ethephon and manual bunch thinning significantly reduced crop, with Borraçal's yield falling about 41% against control.
Ethephon at berry buckshot size lifted sugar and lowered acidity in Loureiro, but gave Borraçal no quality gains.

SCIENCE.head: Grenache rootstocks and irrigation shape water use and stomatal control in Spain
SCIENCE.summ: Under the context of global change, any decrease in water use by crops is essential, because water is becoming a more and more scarce resource, especially in Mediterranean areas, where grapevines are grown
takeaways: A three-year NE Spain study compared Grenache on three rootstocks, irrigated and non-irrigated, measuring water use efficiency and sap flow.
Non-irrigated vines had higher water use efficiency, and 110-R and 41-B outperformed 161-49 on that measure.
Stomatal control in irrigated vines appeared driven more by hormonal than hydraulic signals, the researchers suggest.

SCIENCE.head: Italian researchers outline viticulture strategies for climate change and biodiversity
SCIENCE.summ: In the globalization conditions possible future scenarios, optimistic and pessimistic are supposed
takeaways: Pisa University researchers say climate change may extend viticulture to higher latitudes and altitudes, requiring more resilient vine genotypes.
Italian regions have launched projects to recover abandoned local grape varieties and preserve genetic biodiversity under current legislation.
The authors studied Malvasia of Lazio, Cesanese d'Affile and Cabernet Sauvignon under the Cordon Spur of Conegliano system to cut water use.

SCIENCE.head: Conegliano pruning trials on Lazio grape varieties assess yield, quality and marketing gains
SCIENCE.summ: In this work the salient results of the viticultural and ecomomic researches earned out on interesting italic varieties of Latium (Malvasia of the Lazio and Cesanese d'Affile) and an international vsriety (Cabernet sauvignon), "Cordon Spur of Conegliano" (CSC) as growing system, will be exposed
takeaways: Researchers at the CRA Viticulture centre in Conegliano tested the Cordon Spur of Conegliano system on Lazio grapes and Cabernet Sauvignon.
They compared Vertical Tridimensional Minimal Pruning of Conegliano with and without DMRC double reasoned maturation to raise gross saleable product.
The work targets quality, typicity and originality, with research teams drawn from several Italian universities and agencies.

SCIENCE.head: Vine balance explained: growth versus crop load across the season
SCIENCE.summ: Vine balance is a commonly used term in viticulture that expresses the concept of an appropriate balance of vegetative to reproductive growth of the vine
takeaways: Vine balance means a vine's vegetative growth and reproductive growth are proportionate, enough to ripen fruit and set next year's buds.
Common indirect measures such as yield-to-pruning-weight ratio do not capture how growth balance shifts through the season.
A dynamic carbohydrate simulation model can map seasonal vegetative and reproductive demands against canopy carbon supply.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Video: with Filipa Pato in her old vineyards in Bairrada, Portugal, which she farms with the help of pigs
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Filipa Pato began making her own wines in 2001, starting with three rented plots. Since then she and her husband
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jamie Goode
takeaways: Filipa Pato began making her own wines in 2001 from three rented plots in Bairrada, Portugal.
She and husband William Wouter now farm 20 hectares across 37 plots, mostly planted with the red grape Baga.
Pato uses pigs to regenerate her biodynamically farmed vineyards, some more than 100 years old.

NEWSLETTERS.head: A New White Zin
NEWSLETTERS.summ: If you are not familiar with the lore of White Zinfandel , America’s greatest contribution to wine culture , you are missing out on some excellent cocktail conversation. I understand this might sound like the layup for a bad wine joke, but I’m not being facetious. White Zinfandel is as important to the United States
NEWSLETTERS.author: Tim Atkin MW
takeaways: Tim Atkin argues the US wine industry needs a 'new' White Zinfandel, a cheap, accessible category to revive demand.
He cites US drinkers consuming 49.2 million bottles of White Zinfandel in 2024 despite wine sales being at an all-time low.
He proposes 'Relevé', a field blend of red and white grapes from an entire estate or region, modeled on The Feudal Project's Mrs. Crabtree's blend.

NEWSLETTERS.head: San Francisco’s Local-Wine Complex
NEWSLETTERS.summ: San Francisco and its immediate surrounds have never been more packed with places where a thirsty wine lover can sit
NEWSLETTERS.author: Alder Yarrow
takeaways: San Francisco and nearby areas now host many venues where wine lovers can sit and drink.

NEWSLETTERS.head: A deeper look at underwater wine aging
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Is a wine from the depths ‘better’ or does it depend on the boat?
NEWSLETTERS.author: Miquel Hudin
takeaways: Attis, a winery owned by the Fariña family near Pontevedra, Galicia, ages its Albariño magnums underwater in the O Grove estuary.
Its 2025 Attis Albariño 'Mar' is aged five months underwater at 13-16C, while the 'Standard' bottling of about 120,000 bottles is not.
Laura Vázquez, wife of Robustiano Fariña, said the winery learned early not to use cork and seals its underwater wines with glass caps.

NEWSLETTERS.head: What to Know Before This Year’s Hospices de Beaune Wine Auction
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Discover the world's most famous charity wine auction held since 1859. Get essential tips and insights for this year's legendary Burgundy event
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jonathan Finch
takeaways: The 166th Hospices de Beaune wine sale takes place Sunday 15 November 2026, with the first lot due around 2.30pm under the Halles de Beaune.
The 2026 Hospices crop is small at 432 barrels, 348 red and 84 white, after an early heatwave reduced yields.
Last year's sale raised €18.8 million, with a Grand Cru average of €86,290 per cask and a Premier Cru average of €23,180.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Owendee
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The rituals of service for the holidays, plus this week’s favorite stories about food, wine, and culture
NEWSLETTERS.author: Meg Maker
takeaways: Wine-related search queries slump in July but rise sharply through October, peaking on December 31, according to the author.
The author says the October-December wine-buying season coincides with the Northern Hemisphere harvest.
Resolutionaries swear off wine after New Year's, and wine searches fall sharply afterward.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Visiting the Vineyard in the Sky
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The extraordinary story of Domaine de Beudon in Valais, Switzerland
NEWSLETTERS.author: Simon J. Woolf
takeaways: Marion Granges-Faiss and late husband Jacky farm Domaine de Beudon at 890 metres in Valais, Switzerland, reachable by cable car or a 90-minute hike.
Jacky bought the estate in 1971; it became Valais's first Demeter-certified estate in 1992 after organic conversion in the 1980s.
Since 2003 the only additive is sulphites, with wines bottled unfiltered, though ferments are at Beudon and ageing and bottling happen at Pierre-Antoine Crettenand's Saillon winery.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Inside Chinon’s Lieux-Dits Project
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Vignerons lead a collective effort to recognize the vineyards behind the appellation’s Cabernet Francs
NEWSLETTERS.author: Cab Franc Chronicles
takeaways: Chinon's lieux-dits project, begun by the Chinon Syndicat in 2014, promotes named vineyard sites without a formal classification or hierarchy.
Seven lieux-dits are officially recognized, starting with La Croix Boissée in Cravant-les-Côteaux in 2018 and most recently Vindoux and Les Battereaux in 2025.
Each recognized site gets an in-depth monograph developed with historians, toponymists, geologists and pedologists, plus an engraved stone marking the vineyard.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Yet Another Vintage Port Flex Post (Tasting Selections From 1985 - 2022)
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Last week, I published a bunch of reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the (stellar) 2024 Port vintage. I typically follow those type of posts up with another post of other, older selections of vintage Ports that I tasted at the same event, and I offer them without much shame as simply […] This article was...
NEWSLETTERS.author: Joe Roberts
takeaways: 1WineDude published reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the 2024 Port vintage.
A follow-up post covers older vintage Ports tasted at the same event, spanning 1985 to 2022.

NEWSLETTERS.head: 400 Montepulciano Bottles for Thomas Jefferson circa 1805
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The wine everyone’s been gushing over since the middle ages!
NEWSLETTERS.author: Eveline Chartier
takeaways: A trade contract dated October 17, 1350, between the Del Pecora family and merchant Jacopo di Vanni is the oldest known document for Vino Nobile di Montepulciano.
In 2024 the Consorzio del Vino Nobile di Montepulciano unveiled a document showing the term 'Vino Nobile' was first used in 1766 by the Jesuits.
Thomas Jefferson received 473 bottles of Montepulciano in November 1805 and requested 400 more annually, reportedly from the Jesuit vineyards.
